subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the area of the region bounded by y² = 4ax and x² = 4by.

mark_split.label: Solve for the points of intersection
Identify the upper and lower curves

insider_note: Setting a = b = 1 in the final answer 16ab/3 gives 16/3, which is the area between y² = 4x and x² = 4y — a fast way to check this general-parameter result is consistent.

steps.label: Solve for the points of intersection
steps.margin_note: One mark. Same elimination method as the a = b = 1 case, now carrying a and b through the algebra.
steps.memory_tip: 64ab² inside a cube root always simplifies because 64 is a perfect cube (4³) — pull that out first.
steps.why: Eliminating y between the two equations, the same way as the numeric a=b=1 version, leaves a single equation in x whose nonzero root involves a cube root because the elimination raises x to the fourth power against a linear term.
common_mistakes: Not recognising 64 = 4³, which is what lets x³ = 64ab² simplify to x = 4(ab²)^(1/3).
Dividing by x and losing the root x = 0.

steps.label: Identify the upper and lower curves
steps.margin_note: One more mark. The picture is the same shape as the a = b = 1 case, now with general labels y² = 4ax and x² = 4by.
steps.memory_tip: y² = 4ax opens sideways (upper curve); x² = 4by opens upward (lower curve).
steps.why: The general-parameter curves keep the exact same shapes as the a=b=1 case (a sideways parabola and an upward parabola meeting at the origin and one other point), so the same picture, now labelled with a and b, shows which curve bounds the region from above.
common_mistakes: Assuming the general and numeric versions look different — the shapes are identical, only the labels change.
Swapping which parabola is the upper boundary.

steps.label: Integrate and evaluate
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Carry a and b through every line of the integration — do not substitute numbers early.
steps.memory_tip: Set a = b = 1 in the final answer as a check — it must reduce to 16/3.
steps.why: The same integration as the numeric case, carried through with a and b as constants, gives two fractional multiples of ab whose difference is 16ab/3 — setting a = b = 1 recovers the area 16/3 between y² = 4x and x² = 4y, confirming the general result.
common_mistakes: Losing track of a or b while raising the upper limit to the 3/2 power.
An arithmetic slip in [4(ab²)^(1/3)]³ = 64ab², since (ab²)^(1/3) cubed returns exactly ab².
